items.stem: A physician resident without an individual DEA registration works in a Massachusetts hospital. The resident is licensed or otherwise authorized to prescribe in the hospital's state-authorized practice, and the DEA-registered hospital has assigned the resident a unique internal identifier for prescriptions using its institutional DEA number. A patient later visits the resident at an UNRELATED private office where the resident has no institutional authorization. Which use of DEA identifiers is correct?

choices.text: Use the hospital DEA registration and resident-specific identifier for both locations because the resident has completed training.
choices.why: Incorrect. The institutional exemption is limited to conduct within the authorized institutional practice.

choices.text: Use the hospital's number at the private office if a hospital pharmacist later verifies the resulting prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsequent verification does not extend an institutional registration to unrelated private practice.

choices.text: Use the hospital's DEA number and assigned suffix for authorized hospital practice, not at an unrelated private office.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1301.22(c) requires institutional authorization, internal identification, and acts within the ordinary course of authorized employment.

choices.text: Issue no hospital prescriptions unless the resident receives an individual DEA registration, despite the complete institutional exemption conditions.
choices.why: Incorrect. The federal rule expressly allows qualifying hospital employees and agents to use the hospital's registration with a specific identifying code.

items.citation: 21 CFR 1301.22(c)(1)–(6); 21 CFR 1306.05; MA applicable prescriptive authority
items.novelty_note: Two locations contrast institutional employment with unaffiliated practice.

items.stem: A Massachusetts physician assistant has a CURRENT TEMPORARY PA license but has not passed the national certification examination for full licensure. At a clinic, the PA prepares a Schedule VI written prescription for a patient. The supervising physician reviews and personally SIGNS it before issuance and it is issued in that physician's name. Assume the physician has prescribing authority, the PA's temporary work is otherwise authorized, and all remaining prescription elements are valid. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The arrangement is impermissible because a temporarily licensed PA is categorically prohibited from preparing any prescription or medication order.
choices.why: Incorrect. 263 CMR 5.06(2) permits preparation under the listed physician approval/signature and name requirements.

choices.text: The temporary PA may sign the prescription in the PA's own name because the supervising physician is reachable for retrospective review.
choices.why: Incorrect. Temporary-license conditions differ from full-license PA issuance and require the physician's authorization/signature before issuance.

choices.text: A temporary PA may use the supervising physician's DEA number as their own registration for any Schedule II drug without prior physician approval.
choices.why: Incorrect. Neither temporary licensure nor the physician's DEA number gives independent controlled prescribing authority.

choices.text: This may meet the temporary-PA pathway because the supervising physician signs before issuance and the order is in that physician's name.
choices.why: Correct. The temporary PA may prepare the order, but supervising physician authorization before issuance and physician-name issuance are required.

items.citation: 263 CMR 5.06(2)(a)–(c) (temporary PA prescriptive order); M.G.L. c.94C §7
items.novelty_note: Separates temporary PA prepared-in-supervising-physician-name from fully licensed PA's own prescriptive authority.

items.stem: A Massachusetts prescriber telephones a community pharmacist seeking a new Schedule II oral prescription for a patient in acute distress. The patient needs the drug immediately, electronic prescribing cannot be completed without clinically harmful delay, and all required verification is possible. The prescriber nevertheless requests a THIRTY-DAY quantity, explaining that it is convenient because the clinic is closing for a holiday. The quantity needed for the emergency period is only TWO days. What is the correct dispensing decision?

choices.text: Dispense the full 30 days because ePrescribing exceptions remove all emergency quantity restrictions.
choices.why: Incorrect. 105 CMR 721.060(B)(1) separately caps the quantity at what is adequate for the emergency period.

choices.text: Dispense only a quantity adequate for the two-day emergency, if the other Schedule II conditions are met.
choices.why: Correct. The short emergency supply is legally distinct from a routine 30-day quantity; documentation and federal follow-up are still required.

choices.text: Refuse any emergency oral Schedule II prescription because a phone call can never create valid authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. 105 CMR 721.060(B) and 21 CFR 1306.11(d) permit qualifying emergencies.

choices.text: Dispense 30 days if the prescriber promises to fax the prescription next week and leave the emergency justification unrecorded.
choices.why: Incorrect. Follow-up does not cure an excessive emergency oral quantity or missing documentation.

items.novelty_note: Emergency basis is valid but quantity is not; separates lawful emergency amount from follow-up clock.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy's authorized pickup agent collects a NEW prescription for a patient who is not at the store. The pharmacy offers access to pharmacist counseling, and the agent says: 'The patient asked me to pick this up, but I did not ask whether she wants counseling.' The cashier proposes recording 'patient refused counseling' solely on that statement. What is the most appropriate response?

choices.text: Record the offer and the agent's response; seek a real counseling decision rather than inventing a refusal.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.18 requires a meaningful offer; M.G.L. c.94C §21A requires reasonable efforts to record an actual failure to accept, not one presumed from pickup.

choices.text: Record the refusal because any agent's collection of a prescription is automatically a patient's refusal of counseling.
choices.why: Incorrect. Receiving the prescription and refusing counseling are distinct, and the agent expressly has no information about the patient's preference.

choices.text: Ask the cashier to perform clinical counseling in lieu of the absent patient and record it as pharmacist counseling.
choices.why: Incorrect. A cashier cannot provide clinical counseling and cannot represent that pharmacist counseling occurred.

choices.text: Assume a printed leaflet by itself proves the agent accepted a pharmacist consultation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Written information is not proof of an actual clinical conversation or a documented refusal.

items.novelty_note: Agents picking up Rx with unknown patient preference differ from prior documented patient refusal.

items.stem: A HIPAA-covered Massachusetts pharmacy receives a patient's records from a federally assisted substance-use-disorder program subject to 42 CFR Part 2, pursuant to valid general written TPO consent. A claims reviewer needs the records for ordinary payment operations. Separately, an attorney sends a subpoena seeking to use the same records AGAINST THE PATIENT in a civil proceeding; no additional patient consent or Part 2-qualified court order exists. Which conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: A lawful Part 2 single TPO consent can allow ordinary treatment, payment and healthcare-operations disclosure and qualifying HIPAA redisclosure.
choices.why: Correct. The 2024 Part 2 rule (compliance Feb. 16, 2026) permits a single TPO consent and redisclosure by a HIPAA-covered recipient subject to limitations.

choices.text: Any ordinary subpoena by itself permits using Part 2 treatment records against the patient because the patient signed a general TPO consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Part 2 separately protects against use in proceedings against the patient without the applicable specific consent or court order and legal process.

choices.text: The original patient TPO consent automatically covers separately maintained SUD counseling notes without additional conditions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Part 2 provides additional consent requirements for specially protected counseling notes.

choices.text: The subpoena for use against the patient needs separate legal evaluation; general TPO permission does not override the Part 2 proceeding restriction.
choices.why: Correct. Part 2 restricts proceeding uses/disclosures even after a general TPO consent.

items.novelty_note: Tests TPO-versus-litigation split in same incoming record, not just medical emergency.

items.stem: A pharmacist with a current community-pharmacy CDTM agreement has a physician referral and consent for an adult's diabetes medication management. At 8:00 a.m. the pharmacist makes a permitted Schedule VI dose adjustment under the protocol; later a new critical finding indicates urgent physician review is needed. The pharmacist documents the medication action but plans to tell the physician only at the next monthly visit. What is required?

choices.text: Wait for the monthly collaborative meeting because the physician signed a CDTM agreement and implicitly delegated all updates.
choices.why: Incorrect. A standing agreement does not waive the regulatory notice period or urgent-communication process.

choices.text: Send a copy only if the patient later requests the physician to receive it.
choices.why: Incorrect. The notification obligation arises from authorized CDTM prescribing rather than a later patient request.

choices.text: Notify the physician within 24 hours, escalate urgent findings sooner, and document the change in the patient record.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 16.03(5)(e)2 imposes a 24-hour copy requirement absent a more urgent situation and requires permanent record documentation.

choices.text: Notify the Board of Pharmacy instead of the physician, because the CDTM law makes the Board the patient's routine treating supervisor.
choices.why: Incorrect. The supervising physician must receive the prescription action; Board communication is not a substitute.

items.novelty_note: Adds urgent development after routine modification, beyond existing straightforward 24-hour case.

items.stem: A qualified Massachusetts pharmacist is about to administer an indicated RECOMBINANT ZOSTER vaccine. The patient has not yet been given the Vaccine Information Statement (VIS) and has not had a pre-administration MIIS check. The patient says, 'You may vaccinate me, but I object to other doctors viewing my vaccination history through MIIS.' Which actions are legally appropriate? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Do not report the new dose to MIIS because the patient objected to sharing with other providers.
choices.why: Incorrect. The patient's sharing objection limits access; it does not remove statutory reporting.

choices.text: Give the appropriate VIS and review MIIS before administering this vaccine under the 2025 Board policy.
choices.why: Correct. Federal VIS duties and policy §IV(E) pre-check (non-influenza/non-COVID vaccine) apply.

choices.text: Report the administered dose to MIIS while processing the patient's objection to broader sharing through the MIIS process.
choices.why: Correct. Massachusetts permits restricting data sharing without opting out of data reporting.

choices.text: Tell the patient the objection is impossible and all MIIS data will necessarily be open to every other provider.
choices.why: Incorrect. MIIS offers an objection/withdrawal-of-objection mechanism limiting other-care-provider access.

items.novelty_note: Combined VIS, pre-vaccine registry check, reporting and separate sharing objection.

items.stem: In Massachusetts, a prescriber treats a patient for chlamydia and issues a second valid, signed partner-treatment prescription marked 'EPT' because the unexamined partner's name is unknown. The patient also asks the pharmacy to dispense a third EPT prescription for the same partner's possible GONORRHEA exposure, based only on Board/DCP Policy 2020-08; no third prescription from an authorized practitioner exists. Which response is most appropriate?

choices.text: Dispense partner medications for both infections because an EPT-marked order automatically covers any STI the patient names.
choices.why: Incorrect. The disease-specific EPT rule is not a blanket prescription or independent pharmacy prescribing grant.

choices.text: Refuse the chlamydia EPT solely because the unexamined partner's name is unknown, despite permitted EPT identifier use.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy can allow an EPT identifier when name/address are unavailable.

choices.text: Substitute the pharmacy's own gonorrhea prescription for the missing practitioner order because pharmacist STI treatment authority is unconditional.
choices.why: Incorrect. Current pharmacist prescribing requires its own authorizations and patient-specific protocol conditions; an unrelated request does not qualify automatically.

choices.text: Dispense the prescribed chlamydia EPT, but obtain authorized assessment rather than create an unprescribed gonorrhea EPT order.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2020-08 provides a pathway for a properly issued chlamydia partner prescription, not pharmacy creation of gonorrhea EPT on request.

items.citation: MA Board/DCP Policy 2020-08 (chlamydia EPT); 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7); M.G.L. c94C §19F separate pharmacist STI authority
items.novelty_note: Tests prescriber-created versus pharmacist-invented EPT, but overlap with E30-193 still needs semantic check.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy stores its QRE event records in a secure centralized cloud system but has NO written CQI program description available at the pharmacy itself. Its manager argues that because QRE records can be kept off-site, the entire CQI description also need not be present. What does 247 CMR 15.04 require?

choices.text: Both the program description and every event record may be removed from the premises with no availability requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation explicitly requires an on-premises written program description.

choices.text: Retain the written CQI program at the pharmacy and keep off-site QRE records securely accessible to the staff.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 15.04(1) and (4) deliberately treat the written program description and individual event records differently.

choices.text: All QRE records must remain exclusively on premises in paper form; cloud storage is never acceptable.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 15.04(4) expressly permits event records to be stored at another site.

choices.text: The pharmacy is excused from maintaining a written program whenever no patient injury has been reported.
choices.why: Incorrect. The CQI program exists to detect and address QREs and is not contingent on a specific injury.

items.novelty_note: Facility file location decision, distinct from old CQI retention/annual training.

items.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy is fully licensed but has NOT enrolled as a certified pharmacy in the FDA Mifepristone REMS. A certified prescriber sends a legitimate mifepristone prescription and confirms a signed Patient Agreement Form. The pharmacy can ship with tracking but has not signed a Pharmacy Agreement Form. Is that enough to dispense?

choices.text: No; the dispensing pharmacy also needs its own REMS certification, irrespective of the prescriber's status.
choices.why: Correct. FDA Mifepristone REMS permits dispensing by a certified pharmacy on a certified prescriber's prescription (or by/under a certified prescriber).

choices.text: Yes, because certification of the prescriber and patient agreement replace the pharmacy's own certification.
choices.why: Incorrect. The REMS imposes separate pharmacy certification for dispensing by a pharmacy.

choices.text: Yes, any registered pharmacy may dispense so long as delivery is tracked and the patient agrees.
choices.why: Incorrect. Tracked shipping is one pharmacy certification capability, not an exemption from the certification program.

choices.text: No retail pharmacy can dispense mifepristone under any circumstances because distribution is always restricted to physician offices.
choices.why: Incorrect. FDA's 2023 REMS modification explicitly allows certified retail pharmacies.

items.citation: FDA Mifepristone REMS Pharmacy Agreement / Prescriber Agreement; FDA Q&A current Nov. 2026
items.novelty_note: Separate REMS actor certification, not already-tested four-day shipment threshold.
